title: Can you find the right buckets for these 20 quick case prompts?
description: Twenty short case prompts with the buckets a strong candidate might use. Cover the answer, try your own, then compare.
hook: Yes, and doing it quickly is the point: these 20 short prompts train you to spot the type of case and name three or four tailored buckets in under a minute. Read each prompt, cover the answer, say your buckets out loud, then open the model, which gives the buckets and the one to start with. The timing routine and scoring guide at the end turn the set into a proper drill.
body:
How to use this set

Aim for about 60 seconds per prompt: ten seconds to name the type of case, forty to say three or four buckets, and ten to say where you would start. This is faster than a real interview on purpose. It builds the reflex that lets you spend your interview time on tailoring, not on finding a shape. Many of these prompts appear in longer form, with full model structures, in the themed sets such as profitability and growth.

Prompts 1 to 10

1. A national bank's mortgage applications are down 20%. Why?

Show the buckets
  • Market (interest rates, house prices, transactions)
  • Our pricing against rivals
  • Channels (brokers, online, branches)
  • Approval process (speed, strictness)

Start with: the market. Is everyone down 20%?

2. Should a hotel group launch a budget brand?

Show the buckets
  • Market attractiveness
  • Economics per hotel
  • Cannibalisation of current hotels
  • Capabilities and brand risk

Start with: whether one budget hotel makes money.

3. A hospital's emergency waiting times have doubled.

Show the buckets
  • Demand (volume, case mix)
  • Capacity (staff, cubicles)
  • Process (triage, tests, handovers)
  • Flow out (waiting for ward beds)

Start with: flow out, since blocked beds often back up the department.

4. How should a newspaper grow digital subscriptions?

Show the buckets
  • Reach (traffic, new audiences)
  • Conversion from free to paid (paywall, price, trials)
  • Retention (engagement, bundles)
  • Revenue per subscriber (tiers, add-ons)

Start with: the funnel step with the biggest drop-off.

5. Should a car maker build its own battery plant?

Show the buckets
  • Demand and security of supply
  • Make versus buy economics
  • Technology risk
  • Alternatives (joint venture, long-term contracts)

Start with: cost per kWh, make versus buy, over the plant's life.

6. A fashion retailer's online returns cost too much.

Show the buckets
  • Number of returns (orders × return rate, by product and size)
  • Cost per return
  • Root causes (fit, photos, ordering several sizes)
  • Policy levers

Start with: which grew, the number of returns or the cost of each.

7. Should a city introduce a congestion charge?

Show the buckets
  • Objectives (traffic, pollution, revenue)
  • Impact on residents and businesses
  • Alternatives
  • Implementation (cost, enforcement, politics)

Start with: the objective, which shapes everything else.

8. How would you value a football club?

Show the buckets
  • Revenue streams (media, match-day, commercial)
  • Costs (wages, transfers) and net debt
  • Multiples of comparable deals
  • Strategic premium for this buyer

Start with: how secure the media revenue is.

9. A pharma company's new drug is selling below forecast.

Show the buckets
  • Doctors (awareness, prescribing)
  • Patients (eligibility, adherence)
  • Payers (reimbursement, restrictions)
  • Competition

Start with: payers, since restricted access limits everything downstream.

10. Should an airline start a loyalty credit card?

Show the buckets
  • Customer value
  • Economics (bank payments per point against reward costs)
  • Partner choice
  • Brand risk

Start with: what the bank pays per point.

Prompts 11 to 20

11. A ski resort's profits fell after two warm winters.

Show the buckets
  • Revenue (visitors × spend, by month)
  • Costs (fixed versus flexible)
  • Snow risk (days open, snowmaking, altitude)
  • Other income (summer, events)

Start with: days open.

12. How can a university increase international students?

Show the buckets
  • Markets and demand
  • Offer (courses, fees, rankings)
  • Visas and policy
  • Recruitment channels and conversion

Start with: how many offers turn into enrolled students.

13. A food-delivery start-up is burning cash. What do you cut?

Show the buckets
  • Unit economics per order
  • Marketing efficiency (CAC against customer value)
  • City-by-city profitability
  • Fixed costs

Start with: profit per order by city.

14. Should a supermarket open dark stores for 15-minute delivery?

Show the buckets
  • Demand density
  • Economics per order
  • Cannibalisation of stores and existing online
  • Operations and competition

Start with: economics per order.

15. A government wants more women in the workforce.

Show the buckets
  • Who is out of work and why
  • Barriers (childcare, flexibility, skills)
  • Policy levers and employers
  • Cost and measurement

Start with: segmenting who is out of work.

16. How should an electricity company prepare for rooftop solar?

Show the buckets
  • Lost demand and revenue
  • Grid costs spread over less demand
  • New services (batteries, EV charging, installing solar)
  • Pricing and regulation

Start with: how much revenue is at risk, and how fast.

17. A cinema chain's attendance has not recovered.

Show the buckets
  • Market versus us
  • Film supply
  • Customer experience and price
  • Streaming and home viewing

Start with: whether we are below the industry or the whole market is smaller.

18. Should a coffee brand sell in supermarkets?

Show the buckets
  • Incremental revenue against cannibalisation of cafés
  • Retailer economics
  • Brand risk
  • Operations (roasting, supply)

Start with: net profit after café visits lost.

19. A logistics company's on-time delivery fell to 85%.

Show the buckets
  • Where in the chain (collection, hub, last mile)
  • Capacity against volume
  • Process and systems
  • External factors (weather, partners)

Start with: the step where parcels start running late.

20. How would you increase organ donor registrations?

Show the buckets
  • Awareness
  • Ease of sign-up and defaults
  • Trust and family wishes
  • Channels (driving licences, doctor visits, apps)

Start with: ease, since convenient sign-up points tend to beat campaigns.

Make the drill diagnostic

Once the 60-second version feels easy, slow down to a two-minute version on any prompt: 20 seconds to state the objective, 70 seconds to draw a tailored issue tree, and 30 seconds to give your starting hypothesis and the first piece of data you would ask for. That timing is a practice routine, not an interview rule.

Score each attempt on four things:

  • Complete: could the real answer hide outside your buckets?
  • No overlap: could one cause sit in two buckets?
  • Specific: would your buckets work for any company, or only this one?
  • Prioritised: did you say where to start, and why?

A tree with five elegant headings and no analysis attached scores lower than a simple two-branch tree you could test with data tomorrow. Come back to a prompt a day later without looking at the model. Improvement means your reasoning transfers to new prompts, not that you can recite yesterday's tree.

Where to practise next

Use the structuring drill for fresh prompts against a timer, read MECE explained if your buckets keep overlapping, and when you are ready to use structures in a live case, see practising with a partner.
